column4: “The source section names ق ل ي and glosses it as شدة البغض; Lot calls himself among مِنَ الْقَالِينَ of their deed, giving the same severe aversion a precise object: the act, not its people.

The source section identifies love as a secondary dictionary sense of و ج د; God says وَأَلْقَيْتُ عَلَيْكَ مَحَبَّةً مِّنِّي to Moses, the infant put into the water. The bestowed love is the stated counter-pole to aversion and accompanies protection in the same scene.

The section’s secondary dictionary gloss for و ج د includes الحب; this verse says believers are أَشَدُّ حُبًّا لِلَّهِ, making love an intense orientation toward God. It clarifies the love pole against the section’s شدة البغض, though it is a different relationship and object.

The section’s secondary dictionary note for و ج د includes anger toward a person; 3:119 depicts people biting their fingertips in fury at believers. This gives a specific human hostility that contrasts with the reassurance that God did not reject the Prophet; the verse uses غيظ, not the section’s root.

The source section says the dictionary branch of ء و ي can mean a heart turning tenderly toward someone; Joseph “took his brother close” (آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ) and tells him not to grieve. It makes sheltering an intimate act of compassion toward a distressed person.

The source section’s ء و ي note describes a heart softening in pity; here God’s mercy makes the Prophet gentle to people (لِنتَ لَهُمْ), while a harsh, hard heart would scatter them. This shows tenderness as the social opposite of rejection.

The section’s dictionary glosses for و ج د include love and heart-states, and its note on ء و ي describes a heart turning toward someone. This verse joins welcome for emigrants, love for them, and finding no need in one’s breast; it shows affection enacted as hospitality and selfless care.

The section’s root ء و ي is used for God sheltering an orphan; here the believers recall being few and oppressed, fearing capture, when God gave them refuge (فَآوَاكُمْ), support, and provision. The parallel makes refuge a response to vulnerability.

The section’s dictionary note on ء و ي includes taking someone in; 8:72 names the believers who gave refuge (آوَوا) and aid to emigrants, making shelter a concrete duty toward people forced from home and joining it to mutual protection.

The section’s ء و ي image is shelter offered to someone vulnerable; 8:74 repeats the emigrants and their hosts who gave refuge (آوَوا) and aid, then calls them true believers and promises forgiveness and noble provision. It shows the spiritual weight of receiving the displaced.

The section’s root ء و ي describes taking someone in; the youths “took refuge in the cave” (أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ) and ask their Lord for mercy. Their threatened retreat gives the shelter image another concrete setting.

The section’s root ء و ي is a word for sheltering; the youths tell one another فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ, then say their Lord will spread mercy for them. It links refuge to the tender protection named in the section.

The section connects bestowed love for Moses with the exposed infant in 20:39; this adjacent ayah contributes his return to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she not grieve (وَلَا تَحْزَنَ). It completes the rescue with the mother’s relieved heart.

The section recalls Moses as the baby placed in water when love is cast upon him in 20:39; 28:7 retells his mother’s fearful act of placing him in the river and God’s promise to return him and make him a messenger. It supplies the vulnerable-child scene behind that bestowed love.

The section’s love pole is God’s love cast upon threatened Moses; in this retelling Pharaoh’s wife asks that the child not be killed and calls him a coolness of eyes for them (قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِّي وَلَكَ). Care arises even in the enemy’s household, complicating the scene of enmity.

The section cites God’s love for Moses in 20:39; this parallel account contributes his return to his mother “so her eye may be comforted and she not grieve” (كَيْ تَقَرَّ عَيْنُهَا وَلَا تَحْزَنَ). It completes the image with grief relieved by reunion.

The source section explicitly gives grief (الحزن) as a secondary dictionary sense of و ج د; Jacob’s eyes turn white from grief for Joseph (مِنَ الْحُزْنِ). It makes that hidden emotional face concrete as sorrow at separation.

The source section names grief as a secondary dictionary sense of و ج د; Jacob says he complains of his anguish and grief only to God. This gives grief a direction toward God, rather than treating it as rejection of the one who suffers.

The section’s secondary dictionary gloss for و ج د is الحب; 2:177 says to give wealth عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ to orphans among others. It directly joins love to material care for the vulnerable person whom the section says was sheltered.

The section’s secondary gloss for و ج د includes love; 76:8 describes feeding an orphan عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ. The pronoun’s referent is read as the food or God, but either reading places love beside concrete care for the orphan.

The section’s note on ء و ي describes pity and a softened heart toward someone; in the steep-pass sequence, 90:15 identifies the recipient as a near-relative orphan (يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ), while 90:14 supplies feeding during hunger. The row makes the orphan a specific object of active compassion.

The section glosses ق ه ر as taking by force without the other person’s consent and says رضى can be mutual; this verse bars wrongful consumption of one another’s wealth and allows trade عَن تَرَاضٍ مِّنكُمْ. It states the consent boundary that distinguishes exchange from coercive taking.

The section’s dictionary explanation of ق ه ر is taking without the person’s consent; 4:19 forbids inheriting women against their will (كَرْهًا) and commands decent treatment. It gives a concrete boundary against coercion, parallel to not dominating an orphan.

The section says not to oppress an orphan or take from him without consent; 4:2 commands giving orphans their property and forbids consuming it by mixing it with one’s own. It makes protection of the orphan’s own wealth a concrete form of care.

The section links not coercing an orphan to a person who has been brought to رضى; 4:6 orders guardians to test orphans at maturity and hand over their property when sound judgment appears. It shows the promised return of control to the person whose assets were held.

The section’s dictionary gloss for ق ه ر is coercive taking without consent; 4:10 condemns consuming orphan property unjustly, even describing it as eating fire. It names the material harm that the prohibition on dominating an orphan excludes.

The section’s ق ه ر note highlights taking without the orphan’s consent; 6:152 says not to approach an orphan’s property except in the best manner until maturity. It states the protective limit on a guardian’s power.

The section’s root ق ه ر is glossed as coercive taking; 17:34 repeats the rule not to approach an orphan’s property except in the best manner until maturity. This repeated command makes the consent and stewardship boundary explicit.

The section says the orphan must not be subjected to قهر; 4:127 commands standing for orphan women with justice and names rights withheld from them in marriage/property matters. It shows oppression can be neglect of their claims as well as forceful seizure.

The section sets God’s sheltering of the orphan in 93:6 beside the ban on subjugating him in 93:9; 107:2 describes the one who harshly repels an orphan (يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ). It gives the direct contrary conduct the section’s image rules out.

The section’s orphan image joins being received and protected to the command not to dominate; 89:17 rebukes people for failing to honor the orphan (لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ). It identifies withholding dignity as the opposite of shelter.

The section’s qahr gloss warns against taking from an orphan without consent; 2:220 says that setting their affairs right is best and allows shared household dealings when they are treated as brothers. It distinguishes responsible care from exploitative separation or use.

The section defines ر ض و as the opposite of displeasure; 9:58 contrasts people pleased when given from the charity and angered when not (إِذَا هُمْ يَسْخَطُونَ). The response to a gift makes the section’s turn from displeasure to satisfaction concrete, with its reversal exposed.

The section’s root ر ض و links giving to the recipient’s satisfaction; 9:59 says they would be satisfied with what Allah and His Messenger gave them (رَضُوا بِمَا آتَاهُمُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ) and trusts Allah’s further bounty. It closely parallels gift followed by رضى.

The section pairs a promise of giving with رضى; 92:18 introduces the person who gives wealth to purify himself, whose promised outcome is stated in 92:21. This row supplies the effortful giving behind that parallel promise.

The section says رضى may be brought about after effort; 92:20 says the giver seeks only the face of his Lord, while 92:21 gives the promise that he will be pleased. This row identifies the aim behind the giving.

The section directly compares its promise وَلَسَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضَىٰ with the preceding surah’s وَ لَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ. The parallel also changes the stance: 93:5 addresses the Prophet as recipient of God’s giving, while 92:21 describes the giver who becomes satisfied.
The section quotes 20:130’s instruction to glorify God during the night and day’s ends, لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَىٰ. It links the same promised رضى to worship across the day’s turning points.

The section says the Prophet’s rida is granted through a direction; 2:144 names God’s seeing his face turn toward heaven and promises a qibla تَرْضَاهَا. It makes the inward satisfaction visible as an answered bodily orientation.

The section says رضى can be reached through effort; 2:207 describes a person who offers himself seeking Allah’s pleasure (ابْتِغَاءَ مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ). It gives the reverse movement: a servant strives for the Lord’s رضى.

The section describes a feeling removed from God in 93:3 and a satisfaction given in 93:5; 48:18 says God was pleased with the believers at the pledge under the tree, knowing what was in their hearts, then sent tranquility. It supplies a concrete instance of divine رضى meeting an inward commitment.

The section links divine giving with the recipient’s رضى; 9:72 lists gardens and dwellings for believing men and women, then says Allah’s رضوان is greater. It presents divine approval itself as the greatest gift.

The section defines ر ض و as the opposite of displeasure; 3:162 asks whether one who follows Allah’s رضوان is like one who incurs His سَخَط. It states the boundary between following divine approval and meeting its opposite.

The section explicitly gives رضى as opposite to displeasure; 47:28 says the condemned followed what angered God and disliked His رضوان (وَكَرِهُوا رِضْوَانَهُ). The verse places both poles in one account of a chosen direction.

The section explicitly says رضى can be mutual and quotes this formula; 98:8 says Allah is pleased with them and they with Him (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ), adding that this is for one who fears his Lord.

The section names mutual رضى and cites its formula; 9:100 applies the same “Allah pleased with them and they with Him” to the first emigrants, helpers, and those who follow them well. It shows the reciprocal state in a community.

The section names the two-sided state of رضى; 5:119 repeats that Allah is pleased with them and they with Him after naming the truthful and their reward. It locates mutual approval at the outcome of the judgment.

The section says رضى can run in both directions; 58:22 says Allah is pleased with a people whose hearts He has strengthened in faith, and they are pleased with Him (رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ). It makes the inward orientation and reciprocal relation explicit.
The section quotes this return to God as a state of رضى; 89:28 addresses the soul to return to its Lord رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً, joining the servant’s contentment to being accepted by God.

The section’s emotional image ends with return to God in رضى at 89:28; this preceding ayah identifies the addressed person as the tranquil soul (النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ), supplying the heart-state from which that return is spoken.

The section joins a promised gift to the recipient’s رضى; 89:15 depicts someone treating abundant provision as proof that God has honored him. The following correction in 89:17 matters: this verse contributes the mistaken equation between wealth and worth.

The section’s movement from divine displeasure to رضى is about the heart’s response; 89:16 gives the opposite material condition, restricted provision, and the person concludes that God has humiliated him. The passage’s correction in 89:17 exposes that conclusion as false.

The section connects divine sheltering with the command not to oppress an orphan; after 89:17 rebukes failure to honor the orphan, 89:18 adds failure to urge feeding the poor. This row broadens the same neglect of vulnerable people.

The section’s dictionary note for ق ه ر defines coercive taking without consent; 89:19 condemns devouring inheritance in a single, consuming manner. Beside the rebuke about the orphan in 89:17, it shows how taking can replace care.

The section’s secondary dictionary gloss for و ج د includes الحب; 89:20 says people love wealth with great love, after the passage has condemned neglect of the orphan and devouring inheritance. It sets possessive love against the section’s love expressed as care and giving.

The section says رضى can be mutual and that an orphan must not be coerced; 2:233 allows parents to wean a child by mutual agreement and consultation, then discusses arranging a wet nurse and payment fairly. It joins consent to tender care of a dependent child.

The section defines ق ه ر as taking something without a person’s consent; 4:4 says a wife may remit part of her bridal gift and it may be received only when she gives it willingly. It makes voluntary consent the boundary between a gift and taking.

The section’s dictionary gloss of ق ه ر is coercive taking without consent; 7:127 has Pharaoh’s people announce their domination over the Israelites while planning to kill their sons and spare their women. It gives the violent, powerful sense of the named root that the orphan command forbids.

The section’s ء و ي note describes a heart turning toward and softening for someone; 6:52 tells the Prophet not to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. It makes welcoming the low-status worshiper a concrete counterpart to sheltering the orphan.

The section describes a heart turning tenderly toward another; 18:28 commands patience with those who call their Lord seeking His face and warns against turning one’s eyes away toward worldly adornment. It states the attentional choice that protects humble people from rejection.
The section’s dictionary note for ء و ي evokes a heart turning compassionately toward someone; 80:1 opens with a frown and turning away from a visitor, the opposite bodily and emotional movement.

The section pairs sheltering an orphan with not dominating him; 80:2 identifies the person from whom the speaker turned away in 80:1 as a blind man who came to him. This row specifies the visitor’s vulnerability.

The section’s image contrasts care for the vulnerable with rejection; 80:5 introduces the person who considers himself self-sufficient as the one receiving attention in the exchange begun at 80:1. It supplies the contrasting social position.

The section’s heart-turning image includes compassion for someone vulnerable; 80:6 says attention is given to the self-sufficient man, completing the redirection described in 80:1 while the needy visitor is neglected.

The section says the heart can turn toward someone with tenderness; 80:8 introduces the other visitor, who comes eagerly to the Prophet in the same scene. His active approach makes the subsequent neglect in 80:10 concrete.

The section’s emotional image attends to the heart’s state; 80:9 describes the eager visitor of 80:8 as fearing God. This identifies the spiritual orientation of the person who is nevertheless neglected in 80:10.

The section commands that the orphan not be subjected to harm; 80:10 says the speaker is distracted from the God-fearing visitor introduced in 80:8–9. It completes the scene of turning away from a vulnerable petitioner.

After 107:2 describes repelling an orphan, 107:3 adds failure to urge feeding the poor. The section’s sheltering and non-oppression image thus sits within a wider rebuke of withholding care from the vulnerable.

The section’s note on ء و ي describes pity and a softened heart; 90:14 places feeding on a day of severe hunger at the start of the steep-pass scene. The next ayah, 90:15, specifies a near-relative orphan as one recipient, while this row contributes the urgent act of feeding.

The section’s heart-softening image is enacted toward a vulnerable person; 90:16 identifies another recipient in the steep-pass passage as a poor person in the dust. Alongside the orphan in 90:15, it extends care to the materially exposed.

The section moves from an image of aversion to love and رضى; 60:7 says God may place affection between believers and people with whom they are at enmity. It gives a specific divine reversal from hostility toward affection.

The section traces an emotional direction away from aversion toward رضى; 3:103 recalls people who were enemies until God brought their hearts together and made them brothers. It depicts the same reversal at the level of a community.

The section names love as a secondary dictionary sense of و ج د and cites love bestowed on Moses; 19:96 says the Merciful will establish affection for those who believe and do good. It repeats the specific image of love given by God.

The section’s secondary dictionary gloss for و ج د includes love; 5:54 describes a people whom God loves and who love Him, humble toward believers and firm toward disbelievers. It makes love reciprocal and shows that its expression changes with its object.

The section’s secondary dictionary gloss for و ج د includes love and frames the heart’s changing direction; 9:24 lists family, acquired wealth, trade, and homes as attachments that can be preferred over God, His Messenger, and striving in His path. It gives a concrete boundary for where love is directed.
